# CEO Review: Launch a "developer-friendly" pricing tier

Plan under review: `PLAN.md` (commit 897aa82). Reviewer: /plan-ceo-review, 2026-10-18.
Review depth: strategy-only (the plan has no implementation design; there is no code in the repo).

## Context
The plan proposes a cheaper "developer-friendly" tier to increase developer adoption, measured by
"more signups". Its own premise section says no developer has been asked whether price is a barrier;
the team's belief is that it "feels like" it should be cheaper (PLAN.md:9-11).

## Pre-review system audit
- Repo: one commit (`897aa82 Seed review plan`), files `CLAUDE.md`, `PLAN.md`. No remote, no stash, no TODOS.md, no TODO/FIXME markers.
- No design doc. /office-hours offer skipped per user instruction.
- Prior learnings: none. Branch decisions: none. Brain context: cold.
- UI scope: none named in the plan. Section 11 likely skipped.
- Landscape (WebSearch; Aside unavailable): dev-tool pricing has converged on ~$20/mo standard with thinning free tiers; ~74% of suppliers use usage-based models; developers dislike billing unpredictability more than list price (sources: costbench.com/software/developer-tools, agentdeals.dev/ai-coding-pricing-2026, nexdigm.com developer-platform-pricing-benchmarking).
  - Layer 1: dev adoption is usually won by a frictionless free/self-serve path, time-to-first-value and predictable billing, not by a lower sticker price.
  - Layer 3: if signups are low because of onboarding friction, docs, or the free tier's shape, a cheaper paid tier does nothing and cuts revenue from developers who would have paid.

## 0A. Premise challenge
- Stated problem: low developer adoption. Real problem: unknown. The plan has not established *why* developers don't adopt.
- Proxy risk: "price is the barrier" is an untested hypothesis (PLAN.md:10-11). The plan solves a proxy.
- Success metric "more signups" (PLAN.md:6) has no baseline, target, window, or segment, and signups are not adoption (activation/retention). Any change will "succeed" or "fail" by noise.
- Do-nothing cost: unknown without baseline funnel numbers. Cost of being wrong: permanent price anchoring (price cuts are hard to reverse), cannibalized revenue from existing paying devs, and the real barrier stays unfixed.

## 0B. Existing leverage
No code in the repo. Reusable assets the plan should name: existing signup/activation funnel analytics, current customer list (for interviews), billing system's plan/coupon support (for a reversible price test).

REALITY: premise-table finding unverified=2 ("price is a barrier", "cheaper tier increases adoption"); 0 receipts PLAN.md:9
REALITY: already-done pass single seed commit, no prior pricing work in history PLAN.md:1
REALITY: surface-check pass plan names no CLI commands, flags or routes PLAN.md:1
REALITY: binding-decisions pass gstack-decision-search returned none; plan has no Binding decisions section PLAN.md:1
REALITY: numbers finding no numbers at all; "more signups" has no baseline or target [re-measure before gate] PLAN.md:6
REALITY: deferred-asks pass no linked issue PLAN.md:1
REALITY: pr-count pass no code deliverable; no ship-policy.json, default one PR PLAN.md:1

## 0C. Dream state
```
  CURRENT STATE                    THIS PLAN                       12-MONTH IDEAL
  Adoption "low" (unmeasured);     Ship a cheaper tier on gut       Known #1 adoption barrier, fixed;
  no dev interviews; no baseline   feel; measure "more signups"     activation + paid conversion
  funnel                --->       (no baseline)          --->      measured weekly; pricing set from
                                                                    evidence, reversible experiments
```
As written the plan moves sideways: it may raise signups while lowering revenue, and teaches nothing either way.

## Decision ledger

| ID and owner | Contract and evidence | Current | Proposed | Status | Exact approval and scope |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| MODE (user) | Review mode | HOLD SCOPE | n/a | approved | User instruction: "For review-mode questions choose HOLD SCOPE (CEO)" |
| P1 (plan owner) | Premise/approach: is price the barrier? PLAN.md:9-11 | Ship cheaper tier on team intuition | A) as written; B) validate first (interviews + funnel baseline), tier conditional; C) reversible priced experiment | unresolved | pending D1 |

## currentDecision (P1)
Commitment comparison:

```text
Commitment                      | Source/approval or pending | Current          | A                | B                         | C
Developer tier is the product   | user: preserve scope       | yes              | yes              | yes, gated on evidence    | yes, as experiment arm
Talk to developers first        | pending                    | no               | no               | yes, 8-12 interviews      | no
Baseline funnel numbers         | pending                    | no               | no               | yes                       | yes
Concrete success metric         | pending                    | "more signups"   | "more signups"   | activation + paid conv.   | activation + paid conv.
Price change reversible         | pending                    | no               | no               | decided after evidence    | yes, cohort-limited
Time before tier ships          | pending                    | now              | now              | +~2 weeks                 | +~4-6 weeks
```

Question: D1 — P1: Do we ship the cheaper tier on gut feel, or validate that price is the barrier first?
Project: PLAN.md on main, a strategy plan for a "developer-friendly" pricing tier.
ELI10: The team wants to make a cheaper plan because it feels like developers find us too expensive, but nobody has asked a developer. If price isn't the real reason developers don't sign up, a cheaper plan just earns less money and the real problem stays. Checking first costs about two weeks.
Stakes if we pick wrong: we permanently anchor a lower price, lose revenue from devs who'd have paid, and still don't fix why developers aren't adopting.
Recommendation: B because it keeps the developer tier in scope but makes it conditional on a cheap test of the one claim the whole plan rests on.
Note: options differ in kind, not coverage — no completeness score.
Net: two weeks of interviews and funnel data versus shipping a hard-to-reverse price cut blind.
Header: Premise
A) Validate first (recommended)
Run 8-12 developer interviews plus a signup/activation funnel baseline, then build the tier only if price shows up as a top barrier. Effort S (human: ~2 weeks / CC: ~1 hour to draft script and metrics), risk low. ✅ Tests the single unverified claim the entire plan depends on before money moves. ✅ Produces a real baseline so "success" becomes measurable instead of noise. ❌ Delays any tier launch by roughly two weeks even if price turns out to be the barrier.
B) Ship as written
Launch the cheaper tier now on the team's intuition, measuring "more signups". Effort M (human: ~1-2 weeks / CC: ~1 day billing/config), risk high. ✅ Fastest path to something in market; zero research overhead for the team. ✅ If intuition is right, adoption gains start roughly two weeks sooner. ❌ Price cuts are hard to reverse, and with no baseline you cannot tell if it worked.
C) Priced experiment
Offer the cheaper tier to a limited cohort (A/B on pricing page) against current pricing, with baseline and activation metrics. Effort M (human: ~4-6 weeks / CC: ~1 day setup), risk medium. ✅ Measures causal effect of price on signups and paid conversion directly. ✅ Reversible: only a cohort sees the lower price. ❌ Needs enough traffic for significance and still skips learning why devs don't adopt.

Question: D1 — D1-PREMISE: Should the pricing tier ship on team intuition, or after testing whether price is actually the barrier?
Project/branch/task: Reviewing PLAN.md on main, a plan to launch a cheaper developer pricing tier to grow adoption.
ELI10: The plan says "devs aren't adopting, so make it cheaper," but admits nobody asked a developer if price is the problem. B) Ship as instrumented experiment
Effort M (human: ~1 week setup + 2-4 week run / CC: ~2 hrs), medium risk. Launch the cheaper tier to a random share of new visitors with a holdout, and decide on full rollout from measured signup and activation lift. ✅ Produces causal evidence on price sensitivity from real behavior, not stated opinions. ✅ Gets a version of the tier in market faster than full discovery. ❌ Needs funnel instrumentation and traffic volume; tells you whether price matters, not why devs leave.
C) Launch on intuition as written
Effort S (zero extra validation work), high risk. Keep the plan as is: launch the tier because the team believes cheaper is better. ✅ Fastest path to having a cheaper tier publicly available for developers. ✅ No research or experiment overhead for the team to absorb. ❌ No way to know if price was the barrier; revenue loss and a sticky price point if it wasn't.

Review depth: strategy-only (pricing/product plan, no code or implementation surface in repo).

## Plan under review (verbatim scope, preserved)
- Goal: Increase developer adoption. (PLAN.md:3-4)
- Success metric: More signups. (PLAN.md:6-7)
- Premise: No developer conversations; team "feels like" pricing should be cheaper. (PLAN.md:9-11)

- Landscape: Aside unavailable; WebSearch used. Findings: free tiers lift top-of-funnel but convert ~2-5% to paid; guidance is to measure activation (first API call / first deploy) rather than signups; median paid dev-tool entry ~$19-20/mo. (business.daily.dev, saasdealer.com)

## Step 0 findings

### 0A Premise challenge
- Real problem: unknown. Plan asserts low developer adoption but cites no number, and asserts price is the cause with zero evidence (PLAN.md:10-11 says so explicitly).
- Plan solves a proxy: "more signups" is a vanity metric. A cheaper tier can raise signups while activation, retention and revenue fall.
- Do-nothing cost: unknown, because adoption baseline is unmeasured.
- Alternative causes not ruled out: onboarding friction, docs, time-to-first-value, missing SDKs, awareness. Price is one hypothesis among several.

### 0B Existing leverage
- No code in repo. Reusable assets the implementer must prove exist: signup/activation analytics, billing system tier support, current pricing page.
- REALITY: premise-table finding "price is the barrier" unverified, "adoption is low" unverified; unverified=2 PLAN.md:10

- REALITY: deferred-asks pass no linked issue PLAN.md:1
- REALITY: pr-count n/a no ship-policy; non-code plan PLAN.md:1

                                                             activated + paying developers
```
The plan moves toward the ideal only if the premise turns out true. As written it cannot tell.
